units.text: You love best as an equal, or not at all.

You want a partner with a full life of their own, and you go cold on anyone who needs you to lead. Because standing level is how you feel respected, you keep your own friends, money and plans inside the relationship. You find it harder to be carried, even for a day, than to carry yourself.

Your longest relationships so far have been with people who needed no rescuing, and the partners who leaned on you faded within a season. What you have built from them is a way of loving side by side, with neither of you walking behind.

From your mid-thirties love becomes a partnership of two people who each run their own lives and still choose each other. You learn in these years to lean on a partner without feeling smaller, because you know you can stand on your own feet.

In your late thirties and forties your closest bonds were with people who needed no rescuing, and the partners who leaned on you faded within a season. From those years you built a way of loving side by side, with neither of you walking behind.
Your love runs on sharing, and on keeping count.

You love by sharing, the money and the plans and the friends, and you notice who gets the bigger part. Because a partner is also the person you measure yourself against, small questions of turn and share become contests. You give generously in love and keep a quiet tally of what comes back.

Each relationship of yours so far has pooled what you both had and turned into a race over who put in more. Your eye for an uneven split has sharpened with each of them, along with a soft spot for partners who gave as good as they got.
Your mid-thirties turn love into a team of two, with money and plans divided fairly and every win counted as joint. In these years you stop racing a partner and start racing beside one.

In your late thirties and forties every relationship pooled what you both had and turned into a race over who put in more. Your eye for an uneven split sharpened with each of them, along with a soft spot for partners who gave as good as they got.
You fall for people who widen your life.

In love you fall for the one with plans and friends and somewhere to be. Because range is what draws you, you lose interest within months in a partner who only offers closeness. What you want is someone who brings the world home, and anyone who shuts it out leaves you restless.

The people you have fallen for so far each came with a world attached, a circle of friends or a plan to move or a family that took you in. With each of them, you have stayed a little longer for the life around them than for the person.

From your mid-thirties love and money start to move together. You choose a partner in these years who brings an opening into your life, and the bond holds for as long as the two of you keep heading somewhere new.

In your late thirties and forties the partners you chose each came with a world attached, a circle of friends or a plan to move or a family that took you in. With each of them, you stayed a little longer for the life around them than for the person.
You love best with time alone built in.

You want someone close, and you also want hours each week that belong only to you. Because you work your feelings out in private, you go quiet before a serious talk, and a partner who presses gets less of you. Your love lasts with someone who waits for you to come back.

The people you have loved so far have fallen into two kinds, those who let your private hours be and those who took your silences personally. You have stayed longest with the first kind, the ones who learned that your quiet was thinking and not distance.

The bond you make from your mid-thirties takes your private hours as part of love and not a gap in it. You grow closer in these years by bringing back what you worked out alone, the odd idea or the half-solved puzzle, and letting a partner in on it.

In your late thirties and forties the people you loved fell into two kinds, those who let your private hours be and those who took your silences personally. You stayed longest with the first kind, the ones who learned that your quiet was thinking and not distance.
You love hardest when something is at stake.

You trust a love that has come through something hard, and you feel closest to a partner in the weeks when everything is on the line. Because pressure is how you know a bond is real, you test a partner without meaning to whenever love runs easy. Your kind of partner has the nerve to stand beside you when it counts.

Your relationships so far have been tested hard, by heavy loads and bad stretches carried together, and the strain itself felt like closeness. From them, you have learned to tell a bond that bends under pressure from one that breaks.

Love asks more of you from your mid-thirties, a shared load and the pressure of carrying it well. You come through these years closer to a partner when the two of you turn your strength to the same hard task.

In your late thirties and forties your relationships were tested hard, by heavy loads and bad stretches carried together, and the strain itself felt like closeness. From them, you learned to tell a bond that bent under pressure from one that broke.
You love the person who can answer you back.

You show love by talking and teasing, and a quiet partner leaves you lonely even in a happy home. Since you feel close only when your mind is met, you pick arguments for the thrill of the reply, and some evenings end colder than either of you meant. You want praise and honesty in the same person and rarely settle for half.

The partners you have chosen so far were quick ones who argued well and laughed at the right moments, and each cold spell between you began with honesty that arrived before warmth. You have come out of them knowing which of your true words a partner can take.

Love from your mid-thirties fills with talk, and you look for a partner who matches you word for word. In these years you grow closer through what the two of you argue about, and you learn which of your sharpest words to keep for everyone else.

In your late thirties and forties your partners were quick ones who argued well and laughed at the right moments, and each cold spell between you began with honesty that arrived before warmth. You came out of them knowing which of your true words a partner could take.
You show love by making life easy.

You love by doing, the meal made and the evening kept free and the worry taken off someone's hands. Since giving comfort is how you feel close, you feel most loved by a partner who receives it gladly and gives some back. You give without keeping count and are the last of your friends to notice a partner who only takes.

The relationships that have lasted for you were the easy ones, with partners who enjoyed a slow evening and a good meal as much as you. You have learned from the others, who ate your cooking and gave little back, that ease has to run both ways.

Past your mid-thirties love settles into an easy rhythm with a partner who makes ordinary days pleasant. Your gift for ease comes back to you in these years, as a meal cooked for you or an evening planned around your rest.

In your late thirties and forties the relationships that lasted were the easy ones, with partners who enjoyed a slow evening and a good meal as much as you. You learned from the others, who ate your cooking and gave little back, that ease had to run both ways.
You become the host your family returns to.

Your home is where your family ends up, for meals and holidays and the nights someone needs a bed. Because a full house makes you feel settled, you take on more hosting than anyone asks of you. Relatives treat your door as always open, and you rarely show them how tired you are by the end.

The people you have fed so far have turned into a kind of family, friends who arrive without asking and relatives who want your recipes. You have spent more on food than you could easily afford and counted it as time well spent.

Once you are past your mid-thirties, more of your family gathers at your house, and relatives and friends treat it as a second home. You become the relative everyone means when they say home, and quarrels in the family get settled over your meals.

In your late thirties and forties the people you fed turned into a kind of family, friends who arrived without asking and relatives who wanted your recipes. You spent more on food than you could easily afford and counted it as time well spent.
You love by keeping a life running for two.

You show love by providing, the rent covered and the car serviced before a partner thinks to ask. Because steady provision is how you feel secure, you trust a partner who treats shared money as carefully as you do. You let romance fade when the accounts fill every evening.

The partners who have lasted with you so far cared about upkeep and careful money as much as you did. You have kept the everyday running so well in each of them that you noticed the quiet in the romance only afterwards.

From thirty-five on, love becomes the steadiest thing in your life, a partnership built on joint accounts and savings set aside for both of you. Your warmest seasons in these years are the ones where romance keeps its place beside the upkeep.

In your late thirties and forties the partners who lasted cared about upkeep and careful money as much as you did. You kept the everyday running so well in each of them that you noticed the quiet in the romance only afterwards.
You keep a household that never runs short.

You keep your household running, the cupboards full and the bills paid before they are due. Because a well-kept home is how you show love, you feel uneasy when things at home are left undone. Your family feels safe without knowing how much you do, because you rarely tell them.

In every home you have shared, you have been the one who knows where the spare keys and the papers are. Your careful keeping has carried relatives through lean weeks, with something always put by for whoever needed it.

From your mid-thirties your household runs on what you put by, the savings and the repairs done before anything breaks. You spend these years keeping it stocked and mended, and every lean spell that passes through finds it ready.

In your late thirties and forties you were the one in every shared home who knew where the spare keys and the papers were. Your careful keeping carried relatives through lean weeks, with something always put by for whoever needed it.
You love with promises, and you keep them.

You are drawn to partners with clear values, people who keep their word and expect you to keep yours. Because reliability is what love means to you, you trust slowly and commit fully, and you find casual romance empty. You want a partner you can count on for life and give the same in return.

The relationships that mattered to you have been serious from early on, with plans made and promises kept. You have kept your word in them even after the feeling faded, slow to admit when a promise had outlived the love inside it.

Love settles into something formal and lasting from your mid-thirties, a public commitment and a shared name for what you are. In the small rituals you keep together, you find the warmth that duty alone never gave you.

In your late thirties and forties the relationships that mattered to you were serious from the start, with plans made and promises kept. You kept your word in them even after the feeling faded, slow to admit when a promise outlived the love inside it.
Your home runs on kept promises.

You run your household on clear duties and fair rules, and the people in it know what to expect. Because order is how you protect the people you love, you notice a broken promise at home faster than a kind word. You know your family feels secure with you, and that some of them wish you were less strict.

Your family life has been built on structure, with set routines, shared duties and arrangements that hold. When others forgot, you have been the one who kept the household's promises, and relatives on both sides have come to trust it.

From your mid-thirties you speak for your household, the one who signs, decides and keeps the family's word. You add more warmth to its order in these years, and you find your own house easier to live in than it used to be.

In your late thirties and forties your family life ran on structure, with set routines, shared duties and arrangements that held. When others forgot, you were the one who kept the household's promises, and relatives on both sides came to trust it.
You love the person who makes you feel safe.

You fall for steadiness, the partner who turns up on time and stays calm when you are not. Because being looked after is how you know you are loved, you relax completely with the right person, and you take their care as a given. You are slow to notice how much they carry, and slower to thank them.

The partners who have mattered most to you so far were the ones who looked after you, practically and without fuss. You have handed whole parts of your life to their care, and found afterwards that you had forgotten how to run them yourself.

From your mid-thirties love turns into care that runs both ways, and you learn to give back the patience you once took for granted. You notice what a partner carries for you and take some of the weight yourself.

In your late thirties and forties the partners who mattered most were the ones who looked after you, practically and without fuss. You handed whole parts of your life to their care, and found afterwards that you no longer knew how to run them yourself.
Your home shelters everyone who walks into it.

You make your household gentle, with voices kept low and nobody left out. Because care is what steadies you, you look after the calm at home before anything else, and some arguments get smoothed over without ever being settled. You end most days having looked after everyone in the house except yourself.

Your home so far has been the calm house in your family, where people come to be looked after when things go wrong elsewhere. You have kept its peace with steady care and with the things you chose not to say.

From your mid-thirties the shelter you give starts to work both ways, and a partner looks after you as closely as you look after them. You hold the household together in these years, and you speak up more than you used to.

In your late thirties and forties your home was the calm house in your family, where people came to be looked after when things went wrong elsewhere. You kept its peace with steady care and with the things you chose not to say.
